newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan activists to take islands protest to Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan activists to take islands protest to Tokyo.

text.p: Taiwanese activists on Wednesday pledged to demonstrate at Japan's foreign ministry in Tokyo to protest a landing by Japanese rightists on a disputed island chain in the East China Sea.

But Taiwan's foreign ministry asked the activists to be rational, saying the sovereignty dispute could not be settled in the near term and that the government would talk with Japan to try to resolve the issue.

The activists' announcement came a day after organisers called off plans to sail to the disputed archipelago, known to Chinese as the Diaoyus and Japanese as the Senkakus. They cited a shortage of funds and pressure from Taiwan's government.
The islands are claimed by Japan, China and Taiwan. They lie between Taiwan and Japan's Okinawa island chain.
"We have temporarily called off Sunday's sea protest action. Instead, we will travel to Tokyo and protest outside Japan's foreign ministry," organiser Ching Chia-shou said.
He said ethnic Chinese activists from Taiwan, Hong Kong and the United States would join the Tokyo protest on May 17 or 18.
The activists had planned to sail on Taiwanese fishing boats to the Japanese-administered islands on May 18 and attempt a landing to reassert Taiwan's claim of sovereignty.
The longstanding row over the islands flared when right-wing Japanese lawmaker Shingo Nishimura and supporters landed on one of the uninhabited islands on May 6 and raised Japan's flag.
Ching said his anti-Japanese protest was intended to remind Japan of its history of brutal militarist expansion.
He condemned Taiwan's cabinet-level Council of Agriculture for warning Taiwanese fishermen and fishing companies against leasing boats to the activists.
Activists would stage a landing once they had raised funds and secured boats for their mission, he added.
Roy Wu, Taiwan's foreign ministry spokesman, said the government "affirms patriotism of civilians seeking to defend the country's territory".

"But the sovereignty issue is not something that can be resolved in the near term," he said, adding that the public should understand the government position that it would not give up the Diaoyus but hoped to resolve the issue peacefully.
He said the government had sent a written protest to Japan over the landing issue, and it had called on Tokyo to hold a third round of talks with Taipei.
The sides failed to reach any agreement during their two previous rounds of talks in 1996.

The 1996 erection of a lighthouse on one of the islands by a Japanese rightist group lit nationalist passions in Chinese communities in Hong Kong and Taiwan and sparked a wave of landing attempts, one of which left a Hong Kong activist dead.
